notes:
Photoelectric Effect

  • Work function $\phi_0 = h u_0$ ($ u_0$ = threshold frequency, minimum energy to eject an electron).
  • Einstein's photoelectric equation: $h u = \phi_0 + KE_{max}$, i.e. $KE_{max} = h u - \phi_0 = eV_0$ ($V_0$ = stopping potential).
  • Laws: (1) Photoelectric emission is instantaneous, no time lag. (2) For a given metal, emission occurs only if $ u \ge u_0$; below $ u_0$, no emission regardless of intensity. (3) Saturation photocurrent $\propto$ intensity (at fixed $ u$). (4) Stopping potential $V_0$ depends only on frequency, not intensity; $KE_{max}$ is independent of intensity.
  • Graph of $V_0$ vs $ u$: straight line, slope $= h/e$, intercept on $ u$-axis $= u_0$.

Particle Nature of Light: Photon

  • Photon energy $E = h u = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$; momentum $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{E}{c}$. Photons have zero rest mass, travel at speed $c$, and each interaction is all-or-nothing (particle-like).

Wave Nature of Matter: de Broglie

  • Every moving particle has an associated wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}$.
  • For an electron accelerated through potential $V$: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} = \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}$ nm.
  • De Broglie wavelength decreases with increasing speed/momentum; heavier/faster particles have shorter, practically undetectable wavelengths.
  • Davisson–Germer experiment confirmed the wave nature of electrons via diffraction.

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 2 questions: one on Einstein's photoelectric equation / stopping potential graphs, and one numerical on de Broglie wavelength. Remember $KE_{max}$ never depends on intensity — a favourite trap.

questions.q: The work function of a metal is 2 eV. The threshold frequency for photoelectric emission is (take $h = 6.6\times10^{-34}$ J s, 1 eV $= 1.6\times10^{-19}$ J)
In a photoelectric experiment, if the intensity of incident light is increased keeping the frequency constant (above threshold), then
options: maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons increases
questions.explanation: More intensity means more photons per second, ejecting more electrons per second, increasing saturation current; $KE_{max}$ and stopping potential depend only on frequency, not intensity.

questions.q: Light of frequency $8\times10^{14}$ Hz is incident on a metal of work function 2.0 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons is close to ($h = 6.6\times10^{-34}$ J s)
The de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V is approximately
questions.explanation: $\lambda = \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}$ nm $= \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{100}} = 0.123$ nm.

questions.q: If the frequency of incident light on a photosensitive surface is doubled, the stopping potential
questions.explanation: $eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0$, a linear relation with a non-zero intercept ($\phi_0$), so doubling $\nu$ increases $V_0$ but does not simply double it.

questions.q: A photon and an electron have the same de Broglie wavelength. Then they must have the same
questions.explanation: $\lambda = h/p$ for both; equal $\lambda$ implies equal momentum $p$. Their energies differ since photon energy is $pc$ while electron KE is $p^2/2m$.

questions.q: In the graph of stopping potential $V_0$ versus frequency $\nu$ for a given metal, the slope of the straight line is
questions.explanation: From $eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0$, $V_0 = (h/e)\nu - \phi_0/e$; the slope is $h/e$, independent of the metal, verifying Planck's constant experimentally.

questions.q: Which observation from the photoelectric effect could NOT be explained by the classical wave theory of light?
options: Light can eject electrons from a metal
Existence of a threshold frequency below which no emission occurs, regardless of intensity
questions.explanation: Classical wave theory predicts that sufficiently intense light of any frequency should eventually eject electrons by accumulating energy, but experiments showed no emission below a threshold frequency no matter how intense — explained only by Einstein's photon (quantum) picture.

questions.q: An electron and a proton are accelerated through the same potential difference. The de Broglie wavelength of the electron compared to the proton is
options: smaller, since electron mass is smaller
equal, since charge is the same magnitude
larger, since electron mass is smaller
questions.explanation: $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2meV}$; since $m_{electron} \ll m_{proton}$, $\lambda_{electron} > \lambda_{proton}$ for the same $V$.

questions.q: The energy of a photon of wavelength 620 nm is approximately (take $hc = 1240$ eV nm)
Photoelectric emission from a metal surface occurs with a time lag of
questions.explanation: Photoelectric emission is essentially instantaneous ($<10^{-9}$ s), consistent with a single photon transferring its energy to a single electron in one interaction.

questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of a ball of mass 0.1 kg moving with speed 10 m/s is approximately
questions.explanation: $\lambda = h/(mv) = (6.6\times10^{-34})/(0.1\times10) = 6.6\times10^{-34}$ m — far too small to observe, showing why macroscopic objects don't show measurable wave behaviour.

questions.q: In the Davisson–Germer experiment, the key observation that confirmed the wave nature of electrons was
options: diffraction pattern of scattered electrons at specific angles
continuous energy spectrum of scattered electrons
questions.explanation: Electrons scattered from a nickel crystal showed intensity maxima at specific angles, exactly as predicted by treating the electron beam as a wave undergoing diffraction, verifying the de Broglie hypothesis.

questions.q: The stopping potential for photoelectrons from a metal is 2 V when light of frequency $\nu$ is used. The maximum speed of the emitted electrons is closest to (take $e/m = 1.76\times10^{11}$ C/kg)
questions.explanation: $\tfrac12 mv^2 = eV_0 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{2V_0(e/m)} = \sqrt{2\times2\times1.76\times10^{11}} = \sqrt{7.04\times10^{11}} \approx 8.4\times10^{5}$ m/s.

questions.q: Which of the following particles, all having the same kinetic energy, has the largest de Broglie wavelength?
questions.explanation: For the same KE, $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2mKE}$, so $\lambda \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$; the electron has by far the smallest mass, giving it the largest wavelength.

questions.q: A metal surface has work function 1.5 eV. Light of wavelength 300 nm ($hc = 1240$ eV nm) is incident on it. The stopping potential is approximately
questions.explanation: $h\nu = hc/\lambda = 1240/300 \approx 4.13$ eV; $eV_0 = 4.13 - 1.5 = 2.63$ eV, so $V_0 \approx 2.6$ V.

questions.q: The work function of a metal is 2 eV. Its threshold wavelength is close to ($hc = 1240$ eV nm)
The saturation photocurrent produced by a small point source of light at a photosensitive surface varies with distance $r$ from the source as
questions.explanation: The intensity of light from a point source falls off as $1/r^2$; since saturation current is proportional to intensity (number of photons per second), it too varies as $1/r^2$.

questions.q: In the I-V characteristic of a photocell for a fixed frequency of light, as the retarding potential is increased beyond the stopping potential $V_0$, the photocurrent
questions.explanation: At and beyond the stopping potential, even the most energetic photoelectrons are turned back, so the photocurrent stays at zero.

questions.q: In a photoelectric experiment, the graph of stopping potential $V_0$ versus frequency $\nu$ is a straight line of slope $4.14\times10^{-15}$ V s. The value of Planck's constant obtained from this is approximately
questions.explanation: Slope of the $V_0$ vs $\nu$ graph is $h/e$, so $h = e\times\text{slope} = 1.6\times10^{-19}\times4.14\times10^{-15} \approx 6.6\times10^{-34}$ J s.

questions.q: A 100 W sodium lamp radiates light of wavelength 590 nm uniformly in all directions. The number of photons emitted per second is approximately (take $hc \approx 1.99\times10^{-25}$ J m)
questions.explanation: Energy per photon $= hc/\lambda = 1.99\times10^{-25}/5.9\times10^{-7} \approx 3.37\times10^{-19}$ J. Number of photons per second $= 100/3.37\times10^{-19} \approx 3\times10^{20}$.

questions.q: Metals P and Q have threshold wavelengths 300 nm and 500 nm respectively. Which has the greater work function?
options: Q, since a larger wavelength corresponds to more energy
P, since a smaller threshold wavelength means a larger threshold frequency and hence a larger $\phi_0$
Cannot be determined from this data
questions.explanation: $\phi_0 = hc/\lambda_0$, so a smaller threshold wavelength gives a larger work function; P (300 nm) has the greater work function.

questions.q: An electron is accelerated through a potential difference such that its kinetic energy becomes 150 eV. Its de Broglie wavelength is closest to
questions.explanation: $\lambda = \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}$ nm with $V=150$ V gives $\lambda = 1.227/\sqrt{150} \approx 0.1$ nm $= 1$ Å.

questions.q: If the kinetic energy of a moving particle is increased to 4 times its original value, its de Broglie wavelength
questions.explanation: $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2mE}$, so $\lambda \propto 1/\sqrt{E}$. Increasing $E$ four-fold makes $\lambda$ half of its original value.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about photons is INCORRECT?
options: Different photons of the same frequency can have different energies
Photons travel with speed $c$ in vacuum
questions.explanation: All photons of a given frequency have exactly the same energy $h\nu$; the statement that they can differ is incorrect.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the photoelectric effect is correct?
options: Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons increases with the intensity of incident light
The threshold frequency of a metal depends on the intensity of the incident light
Photoelectric current depends only on the frequency of incident light
Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is independent of intensity but depends on frequency
questions.explanation: By Einstein's equation $KE_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0$, the maximum kinetic energy depends only on frequency and the metal's work function, never on intensity.

questions.q: A metal has a threshold wavelength of 300 nm. Light of wavelength 200 nm is incident on it. The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is approximately ($hc = 1240$ eV nm)

A proton and an alpha particle are accelerated through the same potential difference and have the same kinetic energy afterwards. If the proton's de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda$, the alpha particle's de Broglie wavelength (mass = 4 times the proton's mass) for the same kinetic energy is
questions.explanation: For the same kinetic energy, $\lambda \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$; since the alpha particle's mass is 4 times the proton's, its wavelength is $\lambda/\sqrt{4} = \lambda/2$.

questions.q: In a photoelectric experiment, if the intensity of the incident light is increased while its frequency is kept fixed (above threshold), the I-V graph shows
options: both stopping potential and saturation current increasing
a higher stopping potential, but the same saturation current
the same stopping potential, but a higher saturation current
questions.explanation: Stopping potential depends only on frequency, so it stays the same; more intense light means more photons per second, raising the saturation current.

questions.q: In a photoelectric experiment, if the frequency of the incident light is increased while its intensity is kept fixed (above threshold), the I-V graph shows
options: the same stopping potential as before
the same saturation current, but a larger (more negative) stopping potential
questions.explanation: At the same intensity, the same number of photons arrive per second, so saturation current stays the same; but higher frequency gives photoelectrons more kinetic energy, requiring a larger stopping potential to halt them.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly ranks the photon energies of red, green, and violet light?
questions.explanation: Photon energy $E = hc/\lambda$. Since $\lambda_{red} > \lambda_{green} > \lambda_{violet}$, the energies satisfy $E_{red} < E_{green} < E_{violet}$.

questions.q: The threshold wavelength of a certain metal is 400 nm. Its work function is approximately ($hc = 1240$ eV nm)
The photoelectric effect experiment established which of the following about light?
options: Light travels faster in denser media than in vacuum
Light is purely a wave with no particle-like behaviour
Light behaves as a stream of quanta (photons), each of energy $h\nu$
questions.explanation: The threshold-frequency behaviour and instantaneous emission observed in the photoelectric effect could only be explained by treating light as quanta (photons) of energy $h\nu$, as proposed by Einstein.

questions.q: Assertion: The saturation photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident radiation (frequency fixed above threshold). Reason: Each photon can eject at most one electron, and greater intensity means more photons striking the surface per second.
options: Assertion is true, but reason is false
Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion
Both are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion
Both assertion and reason are false
questions.explanation: More intense light delivers more photons per second; since each photon ejects at most one electron (one-to-one interaction), more electrons are emitted per second, increasing the saturation current proportionally.

questions.q: In Einstein's photoelectric equation $KE_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0$, the term $\phi_0$ represents
options: the total energy of the incident photon
the minimum energy needed to just remove an electron from the metal surface
the kinetic energy of the photoelectron
questions.explanation: $\phi_0$, the work function, is the minimum energy required to free the most loosely bound electron from the metal surface, with no kinetic energy left over.

questions.q: Light of intensity $2\times10^{-3}$ W/m$^2$ and wavelength 500 nm falls normally on a photosensitive surface of area 2 cm$^2$. The number of photons striking the surface per second is approximately (take $hc \approx 1.99\times10^{-25}$ J m)
questions.explanation: Power on the surface $= I\times A = 2\times10^{-3}\times2\times10^{-4} = 4\times10^{-7}$ W. Energy per photon $= hc/\lambda = 1.99\times10^{-25}/5\times10^{-7} \approx 3.98\times10^{-19}$ J. Photons per second $\approx 4\times10^{-7}/3.98\times10^{-19} \approx 1\times10^{12}$.

questions.q: The virtually instantaneous emission of photoelectrons (no measurable time lag) is best explained by
options: the particle (photon) picture, where energy transfer occurs in a single one-to-one collision
the wave picture, since energy is spread continuously over the wavefront
resonance absorption occurring over an extended time
the classical continuous-absorption model of light
questions.explanation: In the photon picture, a single photon transfers all its energy to a single electron in one instantaneous interaction, naturally explaining the absence of any time lag, unlike the classical wave model which predicts a measurable delay.

questions.q: A proton and an electron have exactly the same de Broglie wavelength. Which of the two has the greater kinetic energy?
options: Cannot be determined without more information
questions.explanation: Equal wavelength means equal momentum $p$. Since $KE = p^2/2m$ for the same $p$, the lighter particle (the electron) has the larger kinetic energy.
